item.title: Aizu Autumn Festival: A Samurai Procession Through History — Guide
item.description: The Aizu Autumn Festival is one of Tohoku’s largest historical re-enactment events, held each September in Aizu-Wakamatsu. Its centrepiece is a spectacular samurai procession — hundreds of participants in authentic-style armour, including a portrayal of feudal lord Gamo Ujisato, march through the city streets toward Tsurugajo Castle, alongside performances honouring the tragic Byakkotai cadets. The three-day festival also features traditional music, dance and food stalls throughout the historic city centre.

item.title: Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival: A Summer Obon Tradition — Guide
item.description: The Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival takes place during the Obon season in August, when thousands of paper lanterns are lit along the city’s historic streets and around Tsurugajo Castle to honour ancestral spirits, a Buddhist tradition observed across Japan but given a particularly atmospheric setting here. As dusk falls, the warm glow of the lanterns against the castle backdrop and old townscape creates one of Fukushima’s most photogenic summer scenes, accompanied by traditional bon-odori folk dancing in the streets.

item.title: Higashiyama Onsen: Aizu's Historic Geisha Hot Spring Town — Guide
item.description: Higashiyama Onsen, tucked into a wooded river gorge just outside Aizu-Wakamatsu, is one of Fukushima’s oldest hot spring towns, with a history stretching back some 1,300 years. Traditional ryokan line the Yugawa River, several of which retain a small community of working geisha who continue a centuries-old entertainment tradition once enjoyed by Aizu’s samurai elite. The mineral-rich waters and riverside setting make it a relaxing complement to a day exploring nearby Tsurugajo Castle.

item.title: Tsurugajo Castle, Aizu-Wakamatsu: A Samurai Stronghold Reborn — Guide
item.description: Tsurugajo Castle in Aizu-Wakamatsu is one of Japan’s most storied fortresses — the site of a month-long 1868 siege during the Boshin War, when Aizu samurai (including the teenage Byakkotai) made their last stand against imperial forces. The current five-storey keep, rebuilt in 1965 with a distinctive red-tile roof unique among Japanese castles, houses a museum on Aizu’s samurai history, and the surrounding park bursts into roughly 1,000 cherry trees each April.
